reason: The mission's 45-year lifespan, its status as the most distant human-made object, and its interstellar crossing are documented across multiple independent sources.
story: Voyager 1 is the ultimate scale breaker. Launched in 1977, this probe was only built to last five years. Instead, it has survived for nearly half a century, becoming the most distant human-made object in existence. It is now more than 15 billion miles from Earth, traveling through the cold void of interstellar space at 38,000 miles per hour. Voyager 1 was the first to see active volcanoes on Jupiter’s moon Io and revealed that Saturn’s rings were far more complex than ever imagined. Now, its nuclear power is dying. To keep it alive, engineers are shutting down its instruments one by one. As of 2026, only two of its original science tools remain active: a magnetometer and a plasma wave sensor. It communicates across the abyss via the Deep Space Network, with signals taking nearly a full day to reach us. Carrying a golden record of Earth’s sounds, Voyager 1 is our first eternal messenger to the stars.
angle: Built to last only five years, Voyager 1 has survived for over 45 years and traveled 15 billion miles to become the first human object in interstellar space.

claims.claim: Voyager 1 was launched 16 days after its twin, Voyager 2.
Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object from Earth.
The spacecraft entered interstellar space in August 2012.
Voyager 1 was the first spacecraft to reach interstellar space.
The probe is currently over 15 billion miles away from Earth.
Voyager 1 travels at a speed of approximately 17 kilometers per second (38,000 mph).
The mission was originally designed to last only five years.
Voyager 1 discovered active volcanoes on Jupiter's moon Io.
The spacecraft is powered by radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) using plutonium-238.
The probe carries a gold-plated copper 'Golden Record' containing sounds and images of Earth.
As of 2026, only two science instruments remain operational: the magnetometer and the plasma wave subsystem.
NASA communicates with the probe using the Deep Space Network (DSN).
Signals from Voyager 1 take over 17 hours to reach Earth.
Instruments are being turned off one by one to conserve dwindling power.
Voyager 1 reached Jupiter and Saturn sooner than Voyager 2 despite launching later.
Ed Stone served as the mission's project scientist for over 40 years.
Voyager 1 discovered that Saturn's rings are more complex than previously imagined.

disputed: The 2024 workaround involving the deletion of Jupiter code from the 68KB memory bank is mentioned only in S1 and should be treated as a single-account detail.
The exact timing of the interstellar crossing was debated for over a year due to unexpected magnetic field data before the August 2012 date was confirmed.
Reported signal latency varies by source date, with older accounts stating 17 hours and more recent accounts stating over 23 hours.
